newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Koor says Morgan errs, holds just 1.8 pct.
newsitem.headline: Koor says Morgan errs, holds just 1.8 pct.

text.p: A clerical error by U.S. investment bank Morgan Stanley prompted headlines in the Israeli press on Tuesday that an unidentifed shareholder had taken a major stake in Israel's Koor Industries, Koor said.
But the 8.77 percent stake Morgan told the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission it held in Koor, Israel's biggest holding company, is actually a more modest 1.8 percent, Koor said.

A source who closely follows trading in Koor said the purchase was a financial institution topping out a holding it already had. He added that no buyer could have accumulated nearly nine percent of Koor's equity without attracting notice in the market.

In an SEC filing on February 11, Morgan said it held 1,325,560 million shares, or 8.77 percent of Koor, putting it well above the five percent minimum required to file as a major shareholder in the company. In fact, sources said, Morgan acquired that number of American Depositary Receipts (ADRs) -- not shares.
As five ADRs equal one share, Morgan bought about 265,000 shares, or 1.8 percent of Koor, equal to about $25 million at Koor's current share price.
A Morgan spokesman was not available for comment, but in an announcement to the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange on Tuesday, Koor confirmed the error.

"Relying on (information from) newspaper stories today, there was a mistake in the report...filed by Morgan Stanley to the SEC about increasing Morgan Stanley's holdings in Koor Industries shares to a level of 8.77 percent of share capital," the statement said.
"To the best of the company's knowledge and based on media information that was published, the extent of Morgan Stanley's holdings in the company's shares is 1.8 percent of share capital," Koor said.

The mistaken reporting had prompted speculation that Egypt's Kato group or other interests in the Arab world were behind the Morgan purchase. Kato has a holding in Koor, although less than the five percent that has been widely reported, a source said.
"If it's only 1.8 percent of the company it could be anyone," said Keith Phillips of Societe Generale Equities & Derivatives in London. "If it were nine percent, I'd be interested in the story."
